course.title: C++ Mastery
course.subtitle: Complete C++ Engineering Program
course.tagline: Learn Programming. Build Logic. Master C++.
course.description: C++ from the first program to templates, the STL, memory ownership, DSA and multithreading. Twenty-six modules in six stages, ten learning sections each, and every code sample compiled and run with g++ before it ships, so the output beside a lesson is the compiler's real output.
course.standard: C++17 core · C++20 modern · C++23 where g++ 13 supports it
prerequisites: No prior programming required — Module 00 starts from zero
A computer that can run g++ (or the in-browser lab)
outcomes: Read and write complete C++ programs with confidence
Use variables, operators, conditions, loops and functions correctly
Work with arrays, std::string, pointers and references
Explain stack and heap, and manage memory with RAII and smart pointers
Design classes with constructors, encapsulation and invariants
Apply inheritance, composition and runtime polymorphism
Overload operators with correct value semantics
Write templates and use the STL containers and algorithms
Handle errors with exceptions and files with streams
Use modern C++ features from C++11 through C++23
Solve DSA problems and analyse time and space complexity
Build, test and explain a multi-file C++ project

modules.title: Introduction to C++
modules.goal: Write, compile and run your first C++ program, and understand what the compiler and linker each do.

topics.title: Your first C++ program
topics.body: Every C++ program starts at `main`. `std::cout` writes text to the terminal; `<<` sends the value into the stream and `\n` ends the line.

topics.title: Compile, link, run
topics.body: The compiler turns source into an object file, the linker joins it with the standard library, and the loader runs the executable. `g++ main.cpp -o app` does all three.

topics.title: The compiler is your first reader
topics.body: C++ is statically typed: the compiler checks types before anything runs. An `int` occupies four bytes on this compiler, which `sizeof` reports.

topics.title: Comments are ignored by the compiler
topics.body: `//` comments out the rest of the line and `/* ... */` spans lines. Comments document intent; they never change the program, and the compiler discards them before linking.

topics.title: The standard you compiled with
topics.body: `__cplusplus` is a predefined macro that reports the language standard as a number: `201703` means C++17. It is useful when a build must prove which standard produced it.

topics.title: A program needs exactly one main
topics.body: `main` is the entry point the runtime calls; a second definition fails at link time because the symbol would exist twice.

topics.title: Source becomes an executable in stages
topics.body: Preprocessing, compilation, assembly and linking each produce a different file; `g++` runs all four unless told to stop earlier.

topics.title: The toolchain has four stages
topics.body: Each stage has a flag that stops the build: `-E` preprocesses, `-S` emits assembly, `-c` emits an object file and the default links.

topics.title: A comment records the reason
topics.body: The code already says what happens; a comment earns its place by explaining why, as in the tax rule below.

topics.title: A build fails before it runs
topics.body: A compile error stops the pipeline, so no executable exists to run. Reading the first diagnostic is faster than reading the last.

interviewBank.q: What happens between the source file and a running program?
interviewBank.answer: Preprocessing expands includes and macros, compilation translates each translation unit to an object file, the linker resolves symbols against libraries, and the loader maps the executable into memory before `main` runs. A missing function definition fails at link time, not compile time.

interviewBank.q: Why does `main` return an int?
interviewBank.answer: The return value is the process exit status: 0 means success and a non-zero value reports failure to the shell and to whatever script launched the program. `return 0;` at the end of main is implicit, but writing it makes the intent explicit.

interviewBank.q: Why is C++ compiled instead of interpreted, and what does that buy the program?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler translates the whole translation unit to machine code ahead of time, so type errors surface before the program runs and execution needs no interpreter in the loop. That is why a C++ binary starts fast and has predictable performance.

interviewBank.q: What does `#include <iostream>` actually do?
interviewBank.answer: It asks the preprocessor to copy the contents of the iostream header into the translation unit, which declares `std::cout`, `std::cin` and the stream operators. It does not link anything by itself; the linker brings in the standard library implementation.

interviewBank.q: What does the linker do that the compiler cannot?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler translates each translation unit independently and leaves external symbols unresolved. The linker matches those references to definitions across object files and libraries, and reports a missing definition as a link error.

interviewBank.q: Why is a header not the same thing as a library?
interviewBank.answer: A header is copied into the translation unit by the preprocessor and carries declarations; a library is linked object code that provides the definitions. Including a header without linking its library leaves undefined references.

interviewBank.q: What happens when two translation units define the same non-inline function?
interviewBank.answer: The symbol appears twice in the linked program, which violates the one-definition rule and produces a duplicate-symbol link error. Marking it inline or moving the definition to one unit fixes it.

defenseBank.q: A new learner asks why their code does not run after saving the file. What do you check first?
defenseBank.answer: Saving is not compiling. I check whether a compiler was actually invoked and whether the binary they ran is the one just built.
steps: Confirm the compile command and its exit status.
Confirm the path of the binary that was executed.
Read the first compiler error, not the last.

defenseBank.q: Why teach `std::cout` instead of `using namespace std;`?
defenseBank.answer: The `std::` prefix keeps every name visible at its use site and avoids the collisions that a global using-directive invites. For a beginner the extra five characters are cheaper than a name clash they cannot diagnose.

modules.title: Program Structure and Input/Output
modules.goal: Read the parts of a C++ program and take typed input from the user without leaving the stream broken.

topics.title: Reading input with cin
topics.body: `std::cin >> x` skips whitespace and reads one value into `x`. Reading into a string stops at the first space, which is why full names need `getline`.

topics.title: getline reads the whole line
topics.body: `std::getline(std::cin, line)` keeps spaces. Mixing `>>` and `getline` leaves a newline in the buffer, so consume it first.

topics.title: Formatting output
topics.body: `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision` come from `<iomanip>` and control decimals; the setting persists until you change it.

topics.title: Escape sequences you will actually use
topics.body: `\t` inserts a tab, `\n` ends the line, `\\` prints a backslash and `\"` prints a quote. Each sequence is one character in the string even though it is typed as two.

topics.title: Reading fields from a string stream
topics.body: `std::istringstream` behaves like `std::cin` but reads from a string, which makes parsing testable without waiting for a keyboard. `>>` splits on whitespace and converts to the requested type.

topics.title: cin skips whitespace between fields
topics.body: Extraction ignores leading whitespace, which is why two integers separated by spaces can be read one after another.

topics.title: Insertion chains left to right
topics.body: `std::cout << a << b` feeds the stream from each expression to the next, so order of appearance is order of printing.

topics.title: setfill chooses the padding character
topics.body: `setw` sets the width of the next field and `setfill` chooses what fills it; the fill persists after the field is printed.

topics.title: A newline is a character
topics.body: `\n` is one character with code 10, which is why it can be printed as a char and counted like any other.

topics.title: getline keeps the spaces
topics.body: `std::getline` reads up to the delimiter, so a sentence survives intact where `>>` would have stopped at the first space.

interviewBank.q: Why does `cin >> name` lose the second word of a full name?
interviewBank.answer: Formatted extraction treats whitespace as a delimiter: it reads until the next space and leaves the rest in the buffer. `getline` reads to the newline instead, which is the correct tool for a line of text.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `\n` and `std::endl`?
interviewBank.answer: Both write a newline, but `std::endl` also flushes the stream. Flushing every line is unnecessary in most code and costs performance in loops, so `\n` is the default choice.

interviewBank.q: Why does `std::cin >> name` stop at the first space?
interviewBank.answer: The extraction operator treats whitespace as the field separator, so it reads one token. A full line needs `std::getline`, and mixing the two requires clearing the leftover newline first.

interviewBank.q: Why does `std::setw` affect only the next output field?
interviewBank.answer: Width is consumed by the single insertion that follows it, while flags such as `std::left`, `std::fixed` and the fill character persist. That is why an aligned table repeats `setw` per column but sets the alignment once.

interviewBank.q: Why does mixing >> and getline drop the rest of a line?
interviewBank.answer: The extraction stops before the newline and leaves it in the buffer. getline then reads that leftover newline as an empty line, so the newline must be consumed first.

interviewBank.q: Is std::cout unbuffered?
interviewBank.answer: No. Output is buffered and flushed when the buffer fills, when the program exits, or when std::endl or flush is used. That is why a crash can lose output that was written but not flushed.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer std::string over a char array for input?
interviewBank.answer: A std::string grows as needed and owns its storage, so input cannot overflow a fixed buffer. A char array has a compile-time capacity and needs an explicit length limit.

defenseBank.q: A menu program loops forever after a bad input. Explain the cause.
defenseBank.answer: When extraction fails, `cin` sets its failbit and leaves the bad characters in the buffer, so the next read fails immediately. The fix is to detect failure, clear the state and ignore the rest of the line.
steps: Check `if (!std::cin)` after every read.
Call `std::cin.clear()` and `std::cin.ignore(...)`.

defenseBank.q: Why is input validation part of the lesson, not an advanced extra?
defenseBank.answer: A program that trusts its input is a program that corrupts its own state on the first typo. Validation is cheaper to teach at the point of input than to debug later as a mysterious loop.

learn.title: setfill chooses the padding character
learn.body: `setw` sets the width of the next field and `setfill` chooses what fills it; the fill persists after the field is printed.

learn.title: A newline is a character
learn.body: `\n` is one character with code 10, which is why it can be printed as a char and counted like any other.

modules.title: Variables, Data Types and Constants
modules.goal: Choose a type deliberately, know its range and size, and keep values that must not change constant.

topics.title: The numeric types
topics.body: `int` is the default whole number; `double` is the default decimal. `long long` exists because `int` is not guaranteed to hold a large id.

topics.title: char, bool and their limits
topics.body: `char` stores one character code, `bool` stores true or false, and `sizeof` reports the storage each type takes.

topics.title: const and auto
topics.body: `const` makes a name read-only and lets the compiler reject an accidental write. `auto` asks the compiler to deduce the type from the initializer, which is a tool for long types, not for hiding them.

topics.title: auto deduces a type, it does not guess
topics.body: `auto` takes the type from the initializer, so `auto count = 7` is an `int` and `auto ratio = 7.0` is a `double`. An uninitialized `auto` is a compile error because there is nothing to deduce from.

topics.title: constexpr is computed at compile time
topics.body: A `constexpr` function can run during compilation when its arguments are constants, and `static_assert` then verifies the result before the program ever executes.

topics.title: short and long have different widths
topics.body: The standard fixes minimum sizes, not exact ones, so `sizeof` is the honest way to report what this compiler chose.

topics.title: A literal suffix chooses its type
topics.body: `10u` is unsigned and `10L` is long, so the suffix changes the type and therefore the size the program sees.

topics.title: const cannot be reassigned
topics.body: A `const` variable is fixed after initialization; an assignment to it is a compile error rather than a silent change.

topics.title: Assignment can narrow a value
topics.body: Converting a `double` to `int` truncates toward zero and drops the fraction, which is a silent loss unless the code says otherwise.

topics.title: sizeof works on expressions
topics.body: The operand of `sizeof` is not evaluated; only its type matters, so `sizeof(3.14)` is the size of a double.

interviewBank.q: Why is `double` the default for decimals instead of `float`?
interviewBank.answer: `double` has roughly twice the precision and is the type of unsuffixed floating literals, so it avoids the silent rounding that `float` introduces in ordinary calculations. `float` is for storage-sensitive cases, not the default.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between initialization and assignment?
interviewBank.answer: Initialization gives a variable its first value as it is created; assignment replaces a value that already exists. A `const` can be initialized but never assigned, which is why the distinction matters to the compiler.

interviewBank.q: When should a value be `const` instead of `constexpr`?
interviewBank.answer: `const` promises the value will not change after initialization but may be computed at runtime; `constexpr` requires it to be computable at compile time. Use `constexpr` when the value must participate in compile-time checks or array bounds.

interviewBank.q: Why does `unsigned` subtraction wrap instead of going negative?
interviewBank.answer: Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo two to the power of the type width, so subtracting past zero wraps to a huge positive value. That is well-defined, not undefined, and it is exactly why counts that can go negative should be signed.

interviewBank.q: What does this unsigned subtraction print?
What sizes does this report?
interviewBank.answer:
Output:
1 8

interviewBank.q: What does char arithmetic produce?
interviewBank.answer:
Output:
66

interviewBank.q: Why is size_t unsigned?
interviewBank.answer: It represents sizes and indices that cannot be negative, and it is wide enough to address any object. The trade-off is that a subtraction below zero wraps, so loops that count down need care.

interviewBank.q: What is narrowing and why can it be dangerous?
interviewBank.answer: A narrowing conversion loses information, such as double to int or long to short. Braced initialization rejects narrowing at compile time, which is why {} is safer than = for constants.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between const and constexpr?
interviewBank.answer: const promises no change after initialization but may be computed at runtime; constexpr requires a compile-time constant expression, usable for array bounds and template arguments.

defenseBank.q: Why is an uninitialized local variable dangerous even when the program seems to run?
defenseBank.answer: Its value is indeterminate, so reading it is undefined behaviour: the output can change between builds, compilers and optimisation levels. A test that passes today proves nothing about it.
steps: Name the undefined behaviour, not just the wrong number.
Show the fix: initialize at declaration.
Explain why the bug is not reproducible.

defenseBank.q: When is `auto` a bad choice?
defenseBank.answer: When it hides a conversion or an ownership decision the reader needs to see. `auto x = 1.5;` is fine; `auto p = makeWidget();` is only fine if the widget type is obvious from the name.

learn.body: `auto` takes the type from the initializer, so `auto count = 7` is an `int` and `auto ratio = 7.0` is a `double`. An uninitialized `auto` is a compile error because there is nothing to deduce from.

learn.title: constexpr is computed at compile time
learn.body: A `constexpr` function can run during compilation when its arguments are constants, and `static_assert` then verifies the result before the program ever executes.

learn.title: short and long have different widths

learn.title: A literal suffix chooses its type
learn.body: `10u` is unsigned and `10L` is long, so the suffix changes the type and therefore the size the program sees.

learn.title: const cannot be reassigned

learn.title: Assignment can narrow a value

Why is `double` the default for decimals instead of `float`?
interview.answer: `double` has roughly twice the precision and is the type of unsuffixed floating literals, so it avoids the silent rounding that `float` introduces in ordinary calculations. `float` is for storage-sensitive cases, not the default.

interview.q: What is the difference between initialization and assignment?
interview.answer: Initialization gives a variable its first value as it is created; assignment replaces a value that already exists. A `const` can be initialized but never assigned, which is why the distinction matters to the compiler.

interview.q: When should a value be `const` instead of `constexpr`?
interview.answer: `const` promises the value will not change after initialization but may be computed at runtime; `constexpr` requires it to be computable at compile time. Use `constexpr` when the value must participate in compile-time checks or array bounds.

interview.q: Why does `unsigned` subtraction wrap instead of going negative?
interview.answer: Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo two to the power of the type width, so subtracting past zero wraps to a huge positive value. That is well-defined, not undefined, and it is exactly why counts that can go negative should be signed.

interview.q: Why is size_t unsigned?
interview.answer: It represents sizes and indices that cannot be negative, and it is wide enough to address any object. The trade-off is that a subtraction below zero wraps, so loops that count down need care.

interview.q: What is narrowing and why can it be dangerous?
interview.answer: A narrowing conversion loses information, such as double to int or long to short. Braced initialization rejects narrowing at compile time, which is why {} is safer than = for constants.

interview.q: What is the difference between const and constexpr?
interview.answer: const promises no change after initialization but may be computed at runtime; constexpr requires a compile-time constant expression, usable for array bounds and template arguments.

modules.title: Operators and Type Conversion
modules.goal: Use arithmetic, comparison, logical and bitwise operators without falling into integer division or implicit-conversion traps.

topics.title: Integer division and modulus
topics.body: Two ints divide as integers and discard the remainder. Convert one side to `double` when you need the fractional part; `%` gives the remainder.

topics.title: Comparison and logic
topics.body: Comparisons produce bools, `&&` and `||` combine them with short-circuit evaluation, and `!` negates. A chained comparison like `1 < x < 3` does not mean what it looks like.

topics.title: Bitwise operators
topics.body: `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<` and `>>` work on the bits of an integer. They are used for flags and masks, and they are not the same as the logical operators.

topics.title: Integer division and modulus together
topics.body: `/` between two ints truncates toward zero and `%` returns the remainder with the sign of the left operand. The two results always satisfy `a == (a / b) * b + a % b`.

topics.title: Prefix and postfix increment differ
topics.body: `a++` yields the old value and then increments, while `++a` increments and yields the new value. Reading both in one expression is where beginners lose track of the order.

topics.title: Logical AND short-circuits
topics.body: When the left operand is false the right side is never evaluated, which is what makes `if (ptr && ptr->ok())` safe.

topics.title: Relational operators return bool
topics.body: A comparison produces a `bool`, so it can be printed, stored or combined without converting to int first.

topics.title: A left shift doubles the value
topics.body: Shifting left by n multiplies by two to the n, provided the result still fits in the type.

topics.title: Compound assignment combines two steps
topics.body: `x += 5` reads `x`, adds 5 and stores the result, which is exactly one mutation of the variable.

topics.title: The ternary returns one of two values
topics.body: Both branches must have compatible types, and only the chosen branch is evaluated.

interviewBank.q: Why does `7 / 2` print 3 and not 3.5?
interviewBank.answer: Both operands are ints, so the division is integer division and the fractional part is discarded. Making one operand a double, for example `7 / 2.0`, selects floating-point division.

interviewBank.q: When is `static_cast` preferable to a C-style cast?
interviewBank.answer: `static_cast` states which conversion is intended and is checked at compile time for incompatible types, so a reviewer can see it. A C-style cast can silently become a reinterpret_cast, which is much harder to justify.

interviewBank.q: What is operator precedence and why does it matter?
interviewBank.answer: Precedence decides which operator binds first when several appear without parentheses; `*` before `+`, for example. When the intent is not obvious, parentheses are cheaper than a reader re-deriving the table.

interviewBank.q: Why is `static_cast<double>(a) / b` safer than relying on implicit conversion?
interviewBank.answer: It states the conversion at the exact point it matters, so the division is floating point even if both operands are ints. Implicit conversion can happen later than the author expects, leaving integer division in place.

interviewBank.answer:
Output:

interviewBank.q: What do these bitwise results look like?
interviewBank.answer:
Output:

interviewBank.q: What does the ternary choose?
interviewBank.answer:
Output:
zero

interviewBank.q: Why is signed integer overflow undefined behaviour?
interviewBank.answer: The standard does not define a wrapped result for signed overflow, so the optimizer may assume it never happens and transform the code. Unsigned overflow is defined and wraps.

interviewBank.q: What is short-circuit evaluation used for?
interviewBank.answer: It skips the right operand when the left already decides the result, which guards null dereferences and prevents unnecessary work.

interviewBank.q: Why does -17 % 5 give a negative result?
interviewBank.answer: The remainder takes the sign of the left operand in C++, so the result is -2. The division truncates toward zero, which keeps the identity a == (a / b) * b + a % b true.

defenseBank.q: A learner writes `int avg = total / count;` and the average is wrong. What do you ask?
defenseBank.answer: I ask for the types of total and count before touching the formula: if both are integers, the division already lost the fraction before the assignment.
steps: Check the operand types, not the variable being assigned.
Check for a divide-by-zero path.
Convert one operand and re-test with a case that has a remainder.

defenseBank.q: Why are implicit conversions a common source of bugs?
defenseBank.answer: They are invisible at the call site, so a `double` narrowing to `int` or a negative `int` converting to `unsigned` reads like a normal assignment. Braces and explicit casts make the conversion visible.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Integer division and modulus
practice.task: Two ints divide as integers and discard the remainder. Convert one side to `double` when you need the fractional part; `%` gives the remainder.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Comparison and logic
practice.task: Comparisons produce bools, `&&` and `||` combine them with short-circuit evaluation, and `!` negates. A chained comparison like `1 < x < 3` does not mean what it looks like.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Bitwise operators
practice.task: `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<` and `>>` work on the bits of an integer. They are used for flags and masks, and they are not the same as the logical operators.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Integer division and modulus together
practice.task: `/` between two ints truncates toward zero and `%` returns the remainder with the sign of the left operand. The two results always satisfy `a == (a / b) * b + a % b`.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Prefix and postfix increment differ
practice.task: `a++` yields the old value and then increments, while `++a` increments and yields the new value. Reading both in one expression is where beginners lose track of the order.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Logical AND short-circuits
practice.task: When the left operand is false the right side is never evaluated, which is what makes `if (ptr && ptr->ok())` safe.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Relational operators return bool
practice.task: A comparison produces a `bool`, so it can be printed, stored or combined without converting to int first.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: A left shift doubles the value
practice.task: Shifting left by n multiplies by two to the n, provided the result still fits in the type.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: Compound assignment combines two steps
practice.task: `x += 5` reads `x`, adds 5 and stores the result, which is exactly one mutation of the variable.

practice.title: Rebuild from memory: The ternary returns one of two values

modules.title: Conditional Statements
modules.goal: Make decisions with if, else-if, switch and the ternary operator, including range checks and menu selection.

topics.title: if and else-if
topics.body: Only the first true branch runs. Order the ranges from most specific to least, because a later `else if` is only reached when the earlier ones were false.

topics.title: switch needs integral cases
topics.body: `switch` compares one integral value against constant cases. `break` leaves the switch; forgetting it falls through into the next case.

topics.title: The ternary operator
topics.body: `condition ? a : b` picks one of two values and is an expression, so it can initialize a variable. Keep it for short choices; a nested ternary is harder to read than an if.

topics.title: switch falls through without break
topics.body: Cases share code by stacking labels, and execution continues into the next case until a `break` or the end of the switch. That is a feature when intentional and a bug when forgotten.

topics.title: Guard clauses flatten a decision tree
topics.body: Returning early for each rejected case keeps the happy path at one indentation level. The alternative is a pyramid of nested `if`s where the reader must remember every condition to reach the end.

topics.title: Nested if narrows a range
topics.body: Testing the broad range first and the narrow range inside it keeps each condition small and readable.

topics.title: default handles every other value
topics.body: A `default` label catches the values no case matched, so a switch over an open set still has a defined path.

topics.title: break leaves the whole switch
topics.body: Without `break` execution falls into the following cases; with it the switch ends immediately.

topics.title: Conditions combine with AND
topics.body: A compound condition expresses two requirements at once; both must be true before the branch runs.

topics.title: An if without braces takes one statement
topics.body: Braces are optional for a single statement, which is why adding a second line without braces changes the meaning.

interviewBank.q: When should you prefer switch over if-else?
interviewBank.answer: When one integral value is compared against several constant alternatives and each branch is independent: the switch states the intent and the compiler can warn about a missing default. Ranges and non-integral types need if-else.

interviewBank.q: What is the dangling-else problem?
interviewBank.answer: An `else` binds to the nearest unmatched `if`, which may not be the one the indentation suggests. Braces around every branch make the binding explicit.

interviewBank.q: Which types can be used in a `switch` condition?
interviewBank.answer: Integral types and enums, plus `char`. Floating-point values and strings cannot be switched on because the case labels must be compile-time integral constants.

interviewBank.q: When is a chain of `else if` better than `switch`?
interviewBank.answer: When the conditions are ranges or unrelated predicates, because `switch` only matches exact constants. A `switch` over an enum is still clearer when every enumerator is handled.

interviewBank.answer:

interviewBank.answer:
Output:

interviewBank.q: What does the nested ternary return?
interviewBank.answer:
Output:

interviewBank.q: When is switch clearer than an if chain?
interviewBank.answer: When one integral or enum value selects among several exact alternatives, because the compiler can warn about missing enumerators and the intent is visible at a glance.

interviewBank.q: Why do case labels have to be compile-time constants?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler builds a jump table or comparison chain from the labels, so each value must be known before the program runs. A runtime value cannot be a case label.

interviewBank.q: What is the risk of an if without braces?
interviewBank.answer: Only the next single statement is controlled. Adding a second statement later silently moves it outside the condition, which is how dangling-else bugs appear.

defenseBank.q: Explain a menu-driven program to a beginner without showing code.
defenseBank.answer: It is a loop that shows numbered choices, reads the number, runs the matching branch and repeats until the user chooses exit. The loop is the part that keeps the menu alive; switch is only the dispatcher.
steps: Describe the loop and its exit condition.
Describe how a number selects a branch.
Describe what happens for an unknown number.

defenseBank.q: Why validate a range instead of trusting the branch order?
defenseBank.answer: Branch order encodes assumptions about the data. If a negative mark arrives, an ordered ladder may fall into a plausible-looking bucket, so an explicit range check is what makes the failure visible.

topics.title: The for loop
topics.body: A `for` loop names its counter, its bound and its step in one line, which makes the number of iterations readable at a glance.

topics.title: while and a sentinel
topics.body: `while` repeats while a condition holds. A sentinel value, such as -1, ends a read loop without needing to know the count in advance.

topics.title: Range-based for
topics.body: `for (int v : values)` visits each element without an index. Use `const auto&` when the elements are expensive to copy.

topics.title: do-while runs once before checking
topics.body: The body of a `do-while` executes before the condition is tested, so it always runs at least once. That makes it the right shape for "ask once, then repeat while the answer is invalid".

topics.title: Range-based for reads every element
topics.body: `for (int m : marks)` visits each element in order and copies it into `m`; `for (const int& m : marks)` avoids the copy. The loop cannot run past the container because it uses its iterators.

topics.title: A while loop counts down
topics.body: The condition is checked before each pass, so a counter that reaches the limit ends the loop.

topics.title: A for loop can step by two
topics.body: The increment expression is arbitrary, so `i += 2` visits every second value without an extra condition.

topics.title: Nested loops make rows and columns
topics.body: The outer loop selects a row and the inner loop fills it, which is the shape behind every grid and pattern exercise.

topics.title: continue skips one iteration
topics.body: `continue` jumps to the next pass without ending the loop, which is how one value can be filtered out.

topics.title: An accumulator adds every value
topics.body: A variable declared before the loop and updated inside it carries the running total across iterations.

interviewBank.q: When is a do-while the right loop?
interviewBank.answer: When the body must run at least once, such as showing a menu or reading a value before validating it. The condition is checked after the body, so the first pass is unconditional.

interviewBank.q: Why is `continue` sometimes a readability problem?
interviewBank.answer: It skips the rest of the body, so a reader has to hold every earlier continue in mind to know what actually executes. A guard clause or an if-else is often clearer.

interviewBank.q: When would you choose `while` over `for`?
interviewBank.answer: `for` when the iteration count or the counter is the point of the loop, `while` when the loop ends on a condition that is not a counter, such as reading until end of input.

interviewBank.q: Why does a range-based for not need an index?
interviewBank.answer: It iterates with `begin()` and `end()`, so the container supplies the bounds. That removes the off-by-one class of bug and works for containers that have no index at all.

interviewBank.answer:

interviewBank.q: What is a loop invariant?
interviewBank.answer: A statement that is true before and after every iteration, which is how you reason about what the loop has accomplished and why the exit condition gives the right result.

interviewBank.q: Why is a range-based for unsafe while modifying the container?
interviewBank.answer: The loop holds iterators into the container. Adding or removing elements can reallocate or invalidate them, so the iteration may read freed memory.

interviewBank.q: How do you avoid an off-by-one error at the end of a loop?
interviewBank.answer: Decide explicitly whether the bound is inclusive or exclusive, use the container’s size or iterators, and test the empty and single-element cases.

defenseBank.q: A loop never ends. What is your debugging order?
defenseBank.answer: I check whether the condition can ever become false, then whether the counter is modified on every path, including the continue paths.
steps: Print the loop variables on the first few iterations.
Look for a continue that skips the update.
Check for a condition that compares the wrong variable.

defenseBank.q: Why is an off-by-one error so common at boundaries?
defenseBank.answer: Because the two conventions `<` and `<=` differ in exactly one case, and the difference only appears at the last iteration. Naming the bound as a count rather than an index removes the ambiguity.

modules.title: Functions and Recursion
modules.goal: Break a program into functions with clear parameters and return values, and use recursion with a real base case.

topics.title: Declare, define, call
topics.body: A declaration tells the compiler a function's signature; the definition supplies the body. The call site only needs the declaration, which is why headers work.

topics.title: Pass by reference
topics.body: A reference parameter aliases the caller's object, so the function can change it without pointers. `const&` avoids the copy but forbids the change.

topics.title: Recursion needs a base case
topics.body: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and stops at a base case. Without the base case the call stack grows until it overflows.

topics.title: Default arguments fill the gap
topics.body: A default argument is used only when the caller omits that argument; it is written once in the declaration. Defaults must be trailing, so a parameter with a default cannot precede one without.

topics.title: Passing by reference changes the caller
topics.body: A reference parameter is another name for the caller’s object, so writing through it mutates the original. Passing by value would modify only the copy and leave the caller unchanged.

topics.title: A function returns one value
topics.body: The return type declares what the caller receives; returning early is how a function reports a result or a rejection.

topics.title: void means no return value
topics.body: A `void` function still performs work, as this one prints instead of returning a number.

topics.title: Parameters are copies by default
topics.body: Passing by value gives the function its own copy, so changing the parameter leaves the caller’s variable untouched.

topics.title: A function can call another
topics.body: Composing small functions keeps each one testable and lets a later change stay local.

topics.title: Overloads differ by parameter types
topics.body: The compiler picks the overload from the argument types, so the same name can serve an int and a string.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
interviewBank.answer: A parameter is the variable in the function's signature; an argument is the value the caller supplies for it. The distinction matters when explaining overloading and default arguments.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer `const std::string&` over `std::string` for a read-only parameter?
interviewBank.answer: The reference avoids copying the string, and `const` promises the function will not modify the caller's object. For small types such as int the copy is cheaper than the indirection.

interviewBank.q: What is function overloading resolved by?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler matches the call against each declaration’s parameter list and return type is not part of the signature, so two functions cannot differ only by return type. Ambiguous conversions make the call a compile error.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer `const T&` for a read-only parameter?
interviewBank.answer: It avoids copying a large object while still promising the callee cannot modify it, and it binds to temporaries. For small scalars a plain value is usually cheaper than a reference.

interviewBank.q: How does the compiler choose between overloads?
interviewBank.answer: It ranks the conversions needed for each argument and picks the best viable candidate. An exact match beats a promotion, which beats a user-defined conversion; a tie is an ambiguity error.

interviewBank.q: What does inline actually mean today?
interviewBank.answer: It permits the same function definition in multiple translation units and hints that inlining may be worthwhile. The optimizer decides, so inline is not a performance guarantee.

interviewBank.q: Why does deep recursion risk a stack overflow?
interviewBank.answer: Every call keeps a stack frame until it returns, so unbounded depth exhausts the fixed stack. Converting to iteration or adding a base case bounds the depth.

defenseBank.q: A recursive function crashes with a stack overflow. Explain the failure precisely.
defenseBank.answer: Every call keeps a stack frame alive until it returns, so a missing or unreachable base case turns recursion into unbounded stack growth. The program aborts when the stack limit is reached.
steps: Show the base case and why it is not reached.
Trace the argument on the first three calls.
Fix the base case or convert to iteration.

defenseBank.q: When is iteration a better choice than recursion?
defenseBank.answer: When the recursive depth is linear and the problem needs no backtracking: a loop uses constant stack and is easier to reason about. Recursion earns its cost on trees, divide-and-conquer and backtracking.

learn.title: Parameters are copies by default
learn.body: Passing by value gives the function its own copy, so changing the parameter leaves the caller’s variable untouched.

learn.title: A function can call another
learn.body: Composing small functions keeps each one testable and lets a later change stay local.

learn.title: Overloads differ by parameter types
learn.body: The compiler picks the overload from the argument types, so the same name can serve an int and a string.

modules.title: Strings and Text Processing
modules.goal: Work with std::string confidently: build, search, slice, compare and transform text.

topics.title: std::string owns its characters
topics.body: `std::string` manages its own buffer, so it can grow with `+=` and reports its length with `size()`. A C-style `char[]` does neither.

topics.title: find and substr
topics.body: `find` returns the position of a substring or `npos`. `substr(pos, len)` returns a new string, so the original is untouched.

topics.title: Transform every character
topics.body: A range-based loop over `char&` edits the string in place. `std::toupper` needs the character cast to unsigned char to be safe on all inputs.

topics.title: split a string with find and substr
topics.body: `find` returns the position of a character or `std::string::npos`, and `substr(pos, len)` copies a slice. Combining them splits a record without a regular expression.

topics.title: string_view is a non-owning window
topics.body: `std::string_view` stores a pointer and a length, so taking a substring or passing it to a function copies no characters. It is valid only while the underlying string is alive.

topics.title: Strings compare lexicographically
topics.body: `<` compares character by character, so `apple` sorts before `banana` and the comparison is stable across platforms.

topics.title: append grows a string in place
topics.body: `append` adds characters to the existing string instead of creating a third one, which keeps the capacity it already has.

topics.title: erase removes a range of characters
topics.body: `erase(pos, count)` deletes from the middle and shifts the rest left, shrinking the string.

topics.title: length and size report the same count
topics.body: Both return the number of characters; `size` exists so strings share an interface with the other containers.

topics.title: find returns npos when nothing matches
topics.body: A search compares against `std::string::npos`; testing against anything else can silently succeed.

interviewBank.q: Why is `std::string` preferred over `char[]`?
interviewBank.answer: It owns and resizes its buffer, knows its length, supports value semantics and cannot silently overflow the way a fixed array can. A `char[]` remains useful only at API boundaries or for fixed binary data.

interviewBank.q: What does `npos` mean?
interviewBank.answer: It is the constant returned by `find` when nothing matched. Because it is the largest possible position value, comparing against it is the correct test instead of comparing with -1.

interviewBank.q: What does `std::string::npos` mean?
interviewBank.answer: It is the value returned by `find` when nothing matched, defined as the largest representable size type. Comparing against it is the check, not comparing against `-1` by hand.

interviewBank.q: When is `std::string_view` unsafe?
interviewBank.answer: When it outlives the string it points into, or when that string reallocates. It owns nothing, so a dangling view reads freed memory with no warning.

interviewBank.q: When does a string_view become invalid?
interviewBank.answer: When the string it points into is destroyed, reallocated or modified in a way that changes storage. A view owns nothing, so the underlying characters must outlive it.

interviewBank.q: Why is std::string::size() not the number of visible characters?
interviewBank.answer: It returns the number of bytes in the encoding. A UTF-8 code point can take several bytes, so a multi-byte character counts more than once.

interviewBank.q: What is the small-string optimization?
interviewBank.answer: Many implementations store short strings inside the string object itself instead of allocating on the heap, which makes small strings cheap to create and copy.

defenseBank.q: How do you reverse a string without copying it twice?
defenseBank.answer: Swap from both ends inward, or use `std::reverse` on its iterators. Both work in place, so the cost is a linear pass with no second buffer.

defenseBank.q: Why does case handling need a cast to unsigned char?
defenseBank.answer: `std::toupper` and friends require a value representable as unsigned char or EOF; a negative signed char is undefined behaviour. The cast is a correctness fix, not a style choice.

modules.title: Pointers and References
modules.goal: Understand addresses, dereference safely, and choose between a pointer, a reference and a value.

topics.title: Address and dereference
topics.body: `&x` yields the address of x, and `*p` reads the value stored there. A pointer is a variable whose value is an address.

topics.title: A reference is an alias
topics.body: A reference must be bound when created and cannot be rebound. Writing through it writes to the original, which is why swap takes references.

topics.title: Pointers walk an array
topics.body: Array elements are contiguous, so `p + 1` moves to the next element. The one-past-the-end pointer is valid for comparison but must never be dereferenced.

topics.title: std::array knows its own size
topics.body: A `std::array` carries its length in the type, so `size()` is a constant and `at()` checks the index and throws instead of reading past the end.

topics.title: Array decay loses the length
topics.body: Passing a C array to a function passes a pointer to its first element, so `sizeof` inside the function measures the pointer, not the array. The length has to travel as a separate parameter or be fixed in the type.

topics.title: A reference is another name for one object
topics.body: A reference must bind at initialization and never rebinds, so writing through it always reaches the same object. That makes reference parameters a readable way to return results through the argument list.

topics.title: nullptr is a type, not a macro
topics.body: `nullptr` has type `std::nullptr_t` and converts to any pointer type without becoming an integer. `NULL` is usually `0`, which overloads can mistake for an int.

topics.title: A pointer can be reassigned
topics.body: Unlike a reference, a pointer is an object holding an address, so it can point at one variable and later at another.

topics.title: const can qualify the pointer or the pointee
topics.body: `const int*` forbids writing through the pointer, while `int* const` forbids changing where it points.

topics.title: nullptr compares equal to itself
topics.body: A null pointer is falsy, so `if (p)` is the concise check before dereferencing.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a pointer and a reference?
interviewBank.answer: A pointer is an object that stores an address, can be null, can be rebound and needs dereferencing. A reference is an alias bound once, cannot be null and is used with ordinary syntax. Prefer a reference when the argument must exist.

interviewBank.q: Why is dereferencing a dangling pointer undefined behaviour?
interviewBank.answer: The object it points to has ended, so the memory may be reused or unmapped. Reading or writing there has no defined result, and the program can appear to work until the allocator reuses that block.

interviewBank.q: Why does `std::array` not decay when passed to a function?
interviewBank.answer: It is a class object, not a raw array, so passing it by value copies the whole array and passing by reference keeps its type and length. That is why the size is still available inside the callee.

interviewBank.q: When is `std::vector` the better choice than `std::array`?
interviewBank.answer: When the element count is decided at runtime or must grow. `std::array` is for a fixed compile-time size and avoids a heap allocation entirely.

interviewBank.q: What makes a pointer dangle?
interviewBank.answer: The object it points at is destroyed or freed while the pointer still holds the old address. Reading or writing through it is undefined, so lifetime has to outlive every pointer to it.

interviewBank.q: Why can a reference not be null?
interviewBank.answer: A reference must be bound to a valid object at initialization and cannot be reseated, so the language gives it no null state. A pointer is the type to use when "points at nothing" is meaningful.

interviewBank.q: What is a dangling pointer?
interviewBank.answer: A pointer that still holds the address of an object whose lifetime has ended. Reading or writing through it is undefined behaviour, so lifetime must outlive every pointer.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a const pointer and a pointer to const?
interviewBank.answer: A const pointer cannot change its address; a pointer to const cannot change the pointee through it. const int* p is the second, int* const p is the first.

defenseBank.q: How do you explain `*` and `&` without confusing a beginner?
defenseBank.answer: `&` asks where a variable lives, `*` asks what lives at an address. One takes the address, the other follows it, and the pair cancels when used together.
steps: Draw a box for the variable and a label for the address.

defenseBank.q: When is a raw pointer still the right parameter type?
defenseBank.answer: When null is a meaningful value or the pointer is optional and not owned. Otherwise a reference states that the object exists, and a smart pointer states who owns it.

modules.title: Dynamic Memory and RAII
modules.goal: Allocate and release heap memory correctly, then replace manual new/delete with smart pointers.

topics.title: new and delete
topics.body: `new` returns an address on the free store and `delete` releases it. Arrays need `new[]` with `delete[]`; mixing them is undefined behaviour.

topics.title: unique_ptr owns one object
topics.body: `std::make_unique` allocates and transfers ownership to a `unique_ptr`, which deletes the object when it goes out of scope. Copying is forbidden; moving is allowed.

topics.title: shared_ptr counts owners
topics.body: `shared_ptr` keeps a reference count and deletes the object when the last owner goes away. Use it for genuinely shared lifetime, not as a default.

topics.title: unique_ptr frees itself
topics.body: `std::make_unique` allocates and hands ownership to a `unique_ptr`, whose destructor calls `delete`. No manual cleanup remains on the success path or on a thrown exception.

topics.title: shared_ptr counts its owners
topics.body: A `shared_ptr` keeps a control block with a strong count; copying increments it and destruction decrements it, freeing the object at zero. `use_count` reports the current number of owners.

topics.title: make_unique constructs in place
topics.body: It allocates and forwards the arguments to the constructor in one expression, so no raw pointer ever exists to leak.

topics.title: unique_ptr cannot be copied
topics.body: Copying would create two owners, so the copy constructor is deleted; only `std::move` transfers ownership.

topics.title: shared_ptr resets its count
topics.body: `reset` drops one owner; when the count reaches zero the object is destroyed and its memory returned.

topics.title: RAII frees at the end of the scope
topics.body: The destructor runs when the owning object leaves its block, which is why no explicit cleanup is needed.

topics.title: new[] needs delete[]
topics.body: Array allocation and array deletion are different functions; mixing them is undefined behaviour.

interviewBank.q: What does RAII guarantee?
interviewBank.answer: That a resource is released when its owning object's lifetime ends, including during stack unwinding from an exception. The destructor is the release point, so no manual cleanup path can be forgotten.

interviewBank.q: When would you choose shared_ptr over unique_ptr?
interviewBank.answer: Only when several independent owners must keep the same object alive and no single owner can define its lifetime. Exclusive ownership is simpler and cheaper, so unique_ptr is the default.

interviewBank.q: What does RAII mean in practice?
interviewBank.answer: A resource is acquired by an object’s constructor and released by its destructor, so scope and the type system guarantee cleanup. It works for memory, files, locks and sockets alike.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer `make_shared` to `shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
interviewBank.answer: It allocates the object and the control block in one allocation, which is faster and exception-safe. The raw `new` form can leak if an exception occurs between allocation and the smart pointer construction.

interviewBank.answer:
Output:

interviewBank.q: What does this array allocation print?
interviewBank.answer:
Output:

interviewBank.q: What problem does RAII solve?
interviewBank.answer: It ties resource release to object lifetime, so every exit path — including exceptions — runs the destructor. That removes the need to remember cleanup at each return.

interviewBank.q: When would you use weak_ptr?
interviewBank.answer: When one owner must observe an object without extending its lifetime, such as a cache or a back-reference that would otherwise create a shared_ptr cycle.

interviewBank.q: Why is double delete undefined behaviour?
interviewBank.answer: The second delete operates on memory that has already been returned to the allocator, so the program corrupts its own heap state. Setting the pointer to nullptr after delete prevents it.

defenseBank.q: How do you find a memory leak in a small program?
defenseBank.answer: I look for every new and check for a matching delete on all paths, then run the program under AddressSanitizer, which reports the allocation that leaked.
steps: List allocation sites and their release paths.
Check early returns and exception paths.
Rebuild with -fsanitize=address and read the report.

defenseBank.q: Why is `delete p; delete p;` worse than a leak?
defenseBank.answer: A leak wastes memory but leaves the program defined. A double delete corrupts the allocator's bookkeeping, which is undefined behaviour and often crashes somewhere unrelated later.

modules.title: Structs, Enums and Namespaces
modules.goal: Group related data in a struct, give constants a type-safe enum, and keep names from colliding.

topics.title: A struct groups fields
topics.body: A struct is a named collection of fields with independent types. Aggregate initialization fills them in declaration order.

topics.title: enum class is scoped
topics.body: `enum class` keeps its enumerators inside the type name and does not convert to int implicitly, which prevents accidental comparisons with unrelated numbers.

topics.title: A namespace names a region
topics.body: A namespace qualifies its members, so two libraries can both define `print`. Access with `ns::name` rather than importing everything.

topics.title: enum class keeps its names inside the enum
topics.body: A scoped enum requires `Level::High` at every use and does not convert to int implicitly. That removes the collisions and accidental arithmetic that plain enums allow.

topics.title: Structured bindings unpack a tuple
topics.body: `auto [name, marks] = student;` declares one variable per element and binds them to the tuple’s members. It also works on pairs, arrays and simple structs.

topics.title: A namespace avoids a name clash
topics.body: Two functions with the same name can coexist in different namespaces, and the caller chooses with the scope operator.

topics.title: using brings one name into scope
topics.body: A using-declaration imports a single name, which is narrower than a using-directive and easier to reason about.

topics.title: Aggregate initialization fills fields in order
topics.body: Braced initialization assigns members in declaration order, so a missing value becomes zero.

topics.title: A union shares one storage
topics.body: All members of a union start at the same address, so writing one overwrites the others; the size is the largest member.

topics.title: typedef and using name the same type
topics.body: Both create an alias; `using` reads left to right and works with templates, which is why new code prefers it.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class in C++?
interviewBank.answer: The only language difference is the default access: public for a struct, private for a class, and public for inheritance from a struct. Convention uses struct for passive data and class for types with invariants.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer enum class to a plain enum?
interviewBank.answer: It is scoped, so enumerator names cannot collide, and it is strongly typed, so no implicit conversion to int. A plain enum leaks its names into the enclosing scope and converts silently.

interviewBank.q: When is a plain enum still acceptable?
interviewBank.answer: When the names are local to one small scope and implicit integer conversion is convenient, such as indexing a table. A scoped enum is the safer default because it prevents accidental mixing with integers.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class?
interviewBank.answer: Only the default access and inheritance: struct members are public by default, class members are private. Everything else is identical.

interviewBank.q: Why use an anonymous namespace?
interviewBank.answer: Names inside it have internal linkage, so they are visible only in that translation unit. It is the modern replacement for static at file scope.

interviewBank.q: When is a union preferable to separate members?
interviewBank.answer: When only one alternative is alive at a time and memory matters, such as a tagged variant. A union does not track which member is active, so the tag must be stored separately.

defenseBank.answer: When the fields must change together to stay valid. A struct with public fields cannot enforce that, so the invariant belongs behind a class with a constructor and private members.

defenseBank.q: Why avoid `using namespace` in a header?
defenseBank.answer: It injects every name into every file that includes the header, where unrelated code can collide with it. Qualifying names or importing a single name keeps the effect local.

modules.title: Object-Oriented Programming Fundamentals
modules.goal: Model a real thing as a class with private data, public behaviour and a stated invariant.

topics.title: A class owns its state
topics.body: Data members hold the state and member functions define the behaviour. Keeping the data private means every change goes through a function that can enforce the rules.

topics.title: Getters and setters with a rule
topics.body: A setter is only worth writing when it validates. Here the balance cannot go negative, so `withdraw` refuses instead of leaving the object inconsistent.

topics.title: const member functions
topics.body: A `const` member function promises not to change the object, so it callable on a const reference. Reading methods should be const; that is what makes `print(const Account&)` possible.

topics.title: A class enforces its invariant
topics.body: Keeping `balance` private and validating inside `deposit` means no caller can create a negative balance. The public methods are the only way to change the state, so the rule holds everywhere.

topics.title: const member functions promise not to mutate
topics.body: A `const` member function can be called on a const object and may not modify members. Marking the readers const is what lets the rest of the program pass objects by const reference.

topics.title: this points at the current object
topics.body: Inside a member function `this` is the address of the object the call was made on, which is how chaining returns itself.

topics.title: Encapsulation hides the representation
topics.body: Callers see methods, not fields, so the internal type can change without breaking them.

topics.title: Objects can be copied
topics.body: The compiler-generated copy constructor copies each member, which is enough when the members manage themselves.

topics.title: Static members belong to the class

interviewBank.q: What is encapsulation in practice?
interviewBank.answer: It is not just private fields: it is that every state change goes through an operation that preserves the object's invariant. Without the invariant, private data is only hidden, not protected.

interviewBank.q: Why does a getter exist if the field could simply be public?
interviewBank.answer: A getter keeps the representation free to change and lets the class compute the value rather than store it. It also keeps the field read-only from outside while internal code can still update it.

interviewBank.q: What is encapsulation, beyond private members?
interviewBank.answer: It is the guarantee that state can only change through operations that preserve its rules. Private data is the mechanism; a validated interface is the point.

interviewBank.q: What does `this` point to inside a member function?
interviewBank.answer: The object the call was made on, with the member function’s constness applied. It is why `return *this;` enables chaining and why a const member function has a pointer to const.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer a member initializer list to assignment in the body?
interviewBank.answer: Members are constructed before the body runs, so assignment inside the body is a second write; const and reference members cannot be assigned at all. The list also makes initialization order explicit.

modules.title: Constructors, Destructors and Class Design
modules.goal: Initialize objects correctly, understand lifetime and destruction order, and know when the compiler-generated operations are enough.

topics.title: Constructor initialization lists
topics.body: Members are initialized in declaration order, before the body runs. An initializer list is the correct place to set them, and the order in the list cannot override declaration order.

topics.title: A destructor runs at the end of lifetime
topics.body: The destructor releases whatever the constructor acquired. For a stack object it runs at the closing brace, in reverse order of construction.

topics.title: Rule of Zero
topics.body: If a class manages no resource directly, do not write a destructor, copy or move operation: the compiler-generated ones are correct. Write them only when you own a resource.

topics.title: Initialization lists run before the body
topics.body: Members are constructed in declaration order before the constructor body executes, so an initializer list is the only place to construct a const or reference member. Listing them in a different order than declared invites confusion.

topics.title: A delegating constructor reuses another
topics.body: `Box() : Box(0) {}` hands construction to the parameterized constructor, so the default state is defined in exactly one place. This keeps validation from being duplicated.

topics.title: A constructor runs once per object
topics.body: Every object is constructed exactly once, and the constructor’s body is the first code that sees a fully allocated object.

topics.title: Destruction is the reverse of construction
topics.body: Locals are destroyed in reverse order of construction, which is why later objects can still rely on earlier ones.

topics.title: Copy assignment returns the object
topics.body: Returning `*this` lets `a = b = c` chain, and the parameter is a const reference to avoid a copy.

topics.title: explicit blocks an implicit conversion
topics.body: Marking a one-argument constructor `explicit` stops the compiler from turning an int into the class behind your back.

topics.title: A delegating constructor shares the work
topics.body: One constructor can call another, so validation lives in a single place instead of being copied.

interviewBank.q: What is the Rule of Three and why does it exist?
interviewBank.answer: If a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it almost always needs all three, because they all manage the same resource. Getting one right and the others wrong gives double frees or leaks.

interviewBank.q: Why can member initialization order surprise you?
interviewBank.answer: Members are initialized in declaration order, not in the order written in the initializer list. A member that reads another must be declared after it.

interviewBank.q: What is the Rule of Three?
interviewBank.answer: If a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it usually needs all three because they manage the same resource. Modern code often reaches for the Rule of Zero instead by holding a smart pointer.

interviewBank.q: Why is `explicit` used on single-argument constructors?
interviewBank.answer: It blocks implicit conversions from the argument type, so a function taking the class cannot silently accept a raw value. The conversion must be written at the call site.

interviewBank.q: Why can a copy constructor not take its parameter by value?
interviewBank.answer: Taking it by value would require a copy to create the argument, which calls the copy constructor again, recursing without end. The parameter must be a reference, usually const.

interviewBank.q: Why mark a single-argument constructor explicit?
interviewBank.answer: It stops the compiler from converting the argument type into the class implicitly, so a function expecting the class cannot silently accept a raw value.

interviewBank.q: In what order are members initialized?
interviewBank.answer: In declaration order, regardless of the order written in the initializer list. A mismatch between the two is a common source of reading an uninitialized member.

defenseBank.q: How do you decide whether a destructor should be virtual?
defenseBank.answer: If the class is meant to be a polymorphic base and deletion can happen through a base pointer, the destructor must be virtual; otherwise deleting through the base is undefined behaviour.
steps: Ask whether deletion can occur through a base pointer.
If yes, make the base destructor virtual.
Keep non-polymorphic value types non-virtual.

defenseBank.q: Why is Rule of Zero the default advice?
defenseBank.answer: The compiler's copy and move operations are correct for types that own nothing directly. Writing them by hand only adds a chance to get lifetime wrong.

interview.q: Why can member initialization order surprise you?

interview.q: What is the Rule of Three?

modules.title: Inheritance and Composition
modules.goal: Reuse behaviour through a base class or a member, and choose composition when inheritance would be wrong.

topics.title: Public inheritance is an is-a
topics.body: A derived class inherits the base's public interface and can add its own state. Constructors run base first, then members, then the derived body.

topics.title: Composition is a has-a
topics.body: A class can hold another object as a member. Composition keeps the two lifetimes explicit and avoids the fragile base-class coupling inheritance creates.

topics.title: protected is for derived classes
topics.body: `protected` exposes a member to derived classes but not to outside code. Use it for state a derived class genuinely needs, not as a shortcut for public fields.

topics.title: Construction runs base before derived
topics.body: A derived object contains its base subobject, so the base constructor completes first and the derived body runs after. Destruction is the exact reverse: derived first, then base.

topics.title: Composition models HAS-A
topics.body: A `Car` that contains an `Engine` reuses behaviour without inheriting an interface. Composition keeps the two classes independent, which is usually the cheaper relationship to change later.

topics.title: is-a and has-a are different questions
topics.body: Inheritance answers "is a kind of"; composition answers "contains". Choosing the wrong one makes later changes expensive.

topics.title: protected reaches derived classes
topics.body: A protected member is invisible to unrelated code but available to a derived class, which is the middle ground between public and private.

topics.title: Construction runs base then derived
topics.body: The base subobject must exist before the derived body can use it, so its constructor completes first.

topics.title: Destruction runs derived then base
topics.body: The derived part is destroyed first because it may depend on the base, and the base is torn down last.

topics.title: Composition keeps the parts independent
topics.body: A containing class can swap the contained type without changing its own interface, which inheritance cannot do.

interviewBank.q: Inheritance or composition: how do you decide?
interviewBank.answer: If the derived type genuinely is a kind of the base and must be usable through its interface, inheritance fits. If it merely uses the other type's behaviour, composition is safer and does not couple the two hierarchies.

interviewBank.q: What is the diamond problem?
interviewBank.answer: Two base classes sharing a common ancestor give the most-derived object two copies of that ancestor, so a member reference is ambiguous. Virtual inheritance solves it by sharing one base subobject, at a cost in complexity.

interviewBank.q: What does the diamond problem describe?
interviewBank.answer: Two paths to the same base class create two base subobjects, so members are ambiguous and state is duplicated. Virtual inheritance collapses them into one shared base, at the cost of a more complex object layout.

interviewBank.q: Why is composition often preferred to inheritance?
interviewBank.answer: It couples to behaviour rather than to a type hierarchy, so the contained class can be swapped and tested independently. Inheritance is for a genuine IS-A relationship and a stable base interface.

interviewBank.q: Why is virtual inheritance needed in a diamond hierarchy?
interviewBank.answer: Without it, two intermediate bases each contain their own copy of the common base, so members are ambiguous and state is duplicated. Virtual inheritance makes both paths share one base subobject.

interviewBank.q: When is private inheritance useful?
interviewBank.answer: When a class wants to reuse another’s implementation without exposing an is-a relationship. Composition is usually clearer, since private inheritance still couples to the base.

interviewBank.q: Why is composition usually easier to change than inheritance?
interviewBank.answer: A contained object can be replaced or tested independently, while a base class change propagates to every derived class. Inheritance should model a stable is-a contract.

defenseBank.q: Why can deep inheritance hierarchies become fragile?
defenseBank.answer: A change in a base class reaches every derived class, and the derived classes may depend on protected details that were never a contract. Composition keeps that dependency explicit and local.
steps: Count how many classes depend on the base's details.
Name a change that would break them.
Show the composition that would localise it.

defenseBank.q: What does the base constructor run before the derived one?
defenseBank.answer: Construction goes base first so the derived body can rely on a fully constructed base. Destruction goes the other way: derived first, then base.

defense.q: Why can deep inheritance hierarchies become fragile?
defense.answer: A change in a base class reaches every derived class, and the derived classes may depend on protected details that were never a contract. Composition keeps that dependency explicit and local.

defense.answer: Construction goes base first so the derived body can rely on a fully constructed base. Destruction goes the other way: derived first, then base.

modules.title: Polymorphism and Abstraction
modules.goal: Call the right override through a base pointer, design abstract interfaces and avoid object slicing.

topics.title: virtual enables dynamic dispatch
topics.body: A virtual function is chosen by the object's dynamic type, not the pointer's static type. `override` makes a signature mismatch a compile error instead of a silent new function.

topics.title: Pure virtual makes an interface
topics.body: `= 0` makes the function pure virtual, so the class cannot be instantiated and every concrete derived class must implement it.

topics.title: Object slicing loses the derived part
topics.body: Copying a derived object into a base value slices off the derived fields, so the virtual call uses the base version. Pass by reference or pointer instead.

topics.title: virtual makes the call wait for runtime
topics.body: A call through a base pointer to a virtual function dispatches on the dynamic type, so the derived override runs. Without virtual the call is bound statically and always picks the base version.

topics.title: A virtual destructor is not optional
topics.body: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is undefined and skips the derived destructor. Making the base destructor virtual fixes the whole hierarchy.

topics.title: override checks the signature
topics.body: Writing `override` makes a mismatch a compile error instead of a silently separate function that never gets called.

topics.title: An abstract class cannot be instantiated
topics.body: A class with a pure virtual function is a contract: only derived classes that implement it can be created.

topics.title: A base pointer calls the derived override
topics.body: Dispatch follows the object’s real type, so the same call runs different code depending on what the pointer refers to.

topics.title: A virtual destructor frees the derived part
topics.body: Deleting through a base pointer only runs the derived destructor when the base destructor is virtual.

topics.title: dynamic_cast checks the real type
topics.body: A failed pointer cast returns null, so the program can branch instead of invoking undefined behaviour.

interviewBank.q: Why does a polymorphic base need a virtual destructor?
interviewBank.answer: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer runs only the base destructor when it is not virtual, so the derived part is never destroyed. That is undefined behaviour and typically leaks.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
interviewBank.answer: Overloading picks a function by argument types at compile time within one scope. Overriding replaces a virtual function in a derived class and is selected at runtime by the object's type.

interviewBank.q: What is object slicing?
interviewBank.answer: Copying a derived object into a base object by value keeps only the base subobject, so the derived state and overrides are lost. Passing by reference or pointer avoids it.

interviewBank.q: When should a function be pure virtual?
interviewBank.answer: When the base has no sensible implementation and every concrete derived class must provide one. That turns the class into an interface that cannot be instantiated.

interviewBank.q: How does virtual dispatch work at runtime?
interviewBank.answer: Each polymorphic object carries a hidden pointer to its class’s virtual table, and a virtual call loads the function address from that table. The call therefore depends on the object, not the pointer type.

interviewBank.q: Why must an override repeat the base function’s const qualification?
interviewBank.answer: Const is part of the function’s signature, so a non-const version is a different function. Without the matching const, override reports an error and the base version still gets called through a base pointer.

interviewBank.q: Why should a base destructor be virtual or protected?
interviewBank.answer: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is undefined and skips the derived cleanup. A virtual destructor, or a protected non-virtual one, closes that hole.

defenseBank.q: How would you explain polymorphism to a beginner?
defenseBank.answer: One instruction, many behaviours: calling area() on a shape works whether it is a square or a circle, and each type answers in its own way.
steps: Name the shared instruction.
Show two different answers.
Show that the caller did not change.

defenseBank.q: When is runtime polymorphism the wrong tool?
defenseBank.answer: When the type is known at compile time or the hot path cannot afford an indirect call. Templates or plain overloads resolve earlier and inline better.

interviewBank.q: Which operators should stay non-member?
interviewBank.answer: Stream insertion and extraction, and any operator whose left operand is not your type, such as `int + Complex`. They can be friends when they need private access.

interviewBank.q: Why must operator= handle self-assignment?
interviewBank.answer: `a = a` would otherwise free a resource before reading from it. The usual guard checks for `this == &other` before releasing anything.

interviewBank.q: Which operators cannot be overloaded?
interviewBank.answer: `::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:` and `sizeof`. Everything else that takes at least one class-type operand can be overloaded, though doing so should preserve the operator’s expected meaning.

interviewBank.q: Why is `operator=` usually a member function?
interviewBank.answer: It needs access to the object being assigned and must return `*this` by reference for chaining. The compiler-generated copy assignment is a member for the same reason.

interviewBank.q: Why is operator== usually written as a free function?
interviewBank.answer: A free function treats both operands symmetrically and allows a conversion on either side, while a member operator only converts the right operand. It also keeps the class interface smaller.

interviewBank.q: Why must operator= be a member function?
interviewBank.answer: The language requires it, because assignment needs access to the object being assigned and must return *this for chaining.

interviewBank.q: When should a conversion operator be explicit?
interviewBank.answer: When an implicit conversion would be surprising or lossy. Explicit keeps the conversion at the call site, where the reader can see it.

defenseBank.q: Why is overloading `&&` or `,` usually a mistake?
defenseBank.answer: Both have built-in sequencing and short-circuit behaviour that a user-defined overload cannot reproduce, so code that relies on them silently changes meaning.
steps: Name the built-in guarantee.

Keep the operator for types where it is unsurprising.

defenseBank.q: What makes an operator overload defensible?
defenseBank.answer: It behaves like the built-in operator for that concept, has the expected return type and does not surprise with side effects. If a reader has to check the header, it probably should have been a named function.
