modules.goal: Write one function or class that works for many types, and read template errors without panic.

topics.title: A function template
topics.body: The compiler generates a concrete function for each type used, so the same body works for int and double without runtime cost.

topics.title: A class template
topics.body: A class template parameterises the element type. Member functions defined outside the class need the template header and the qualified name.

topics.title: Two parameters, one algorithm
topics.body: Templates can take several parameters. The compiler deduces each from the arguments, and a mismatch between them is reported at the call site.

topics.title: A function template instantiates per type
topics.body: The compiler generates a separate function for each deduced type, so `larger(3, 9)` and `larger(2.5, 1.5)` share source but not machine code. Errors appear at instantiation, not at definition.

topics.title: Non-type template parameters carry a value
topics.body: A template can take a constant value such as `int N`, which lets the size travel in the type. The array reference form below preserves the length instead of decaying to a pointer.

topics.title: Template deduction reads the call
topics.body: The compiler infers `T` from the argument types, so the caller rarely writes the angle brackets.

topics.title: A class template can default its parameter
topics.body: A default argument makes the common instantiation shorter while still allowing another type.

topics.title: A variadic template counts its arguments
topics.body: A fold expression over a parameter pack can consume any number of arguments without recursion.

topics.title: if constexpr drops the other branch
topics.body: The discarded branch is not instantiated, so template code can mention operations that only exist for some types.

topics.title: A template can be specialized
topics.body: A full specialization replaces the generic definition for one concrete type, which is how behaviour is customized.

interviewBank.q: What is template instantiation?
interviewBank.answer: It is the compiler generating a concrete function or class for the types actually used. Nothing is generated for types you never instantiate, which is why template errors often appear at the call site.

interviewBank.q: Why do template errors look so long?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler reports the full instantiation chain from your call down into the library. The useful line is usually the first note that names your type and the requirement that failed.

interviewBank.q: Why must a template usually be defined in a header?
interviewBank.answer: The compiler needs the definition to instantiate it for each type at the point of use. A definition hidden in a .cpp file is invisible to other translation units, producing link errors.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a template and a macro?
interviewBank.answer: A template is type-checked, scoped and instantiated by the compiler. A macro is textual substitution with no type safety, which is why templates replaced most macro-based generic code.

interviewBank.q: What is SFINAE?

modules.title: STL Containers
modules.goal: Choose the right container for the access pattern and use vector, map and set without fighting their interfaces.

topics.title: vector is the default sequence
topics.body: `std::vector` stores its elements contiguously and grows geometrically, so push_back is amortised constant time and iteration is cache-friendly.

topics.title: map keeps keys sorted
topics.body: `std::map` is a balanced tree: lookup is logarithmic and iteration is in key order. `operator[]` inserts a default value when the key is missing, which is sometimes what you want and sometimes a bug.

topics.title: set stores unique keys
topics.body: A `set` removes duplicates and keeps order, so it is the tool for distinct values and membership tests rather than counts.

topics.title: map keeps its keys sorted
topics.body: `std::map` orders keys by `operator<`, so iteration is sorted without an extra sort. Lookup is logarithmic and the container stores one value per unique key.

topics.title: unordered_map counts without promising order
topics.body: The hashed container gives average constant-time lookup, which is why it is the usual choice for frequency tables. Iteration order is unspecified, so never print it as if it were sorted.

topics.title: vector grows geometrically
topics.body: When capacity runs out the vector allocates a larger block and moves the elements, so repeated pushes stay amortized constant.

topics.title: map operator[] inserts a default
topics.body: Reading a missing key with `[]` creates it with a zero value, which is convenient for counters and dangerous for lookups.

topics.title: set rejects duplicates
topics.body: Inserting an existing key changes nothing and reports that no insertion happened.

topics.title: deque pushes at both ends
topics.body: A double-ended queue keeps fast insertion at the front and the back, which a vector cannot do at the front.

topics.title: priority_queue pops the largest
topics.body: The default comparator is `less`, so the top is the greatest element and each pop removes it.

interviewBank.q: vector, list or deque: how do you choose?
interviewBank.answer: Default to vector for contiguous storage and cache locality. Use deque when you need fast insertion at both ends, and list only when stable iterators and frequent middle insertion outweigh the pointer overhead.

interviewBank.q: map or unordered_map?
interviewBank.answer: map when order matters or you need range queries, unordered_map when average constant lookup matters more and the key can be hashed. The unordered version trades ordering and worst-case guarantees for speed.

interviewBank.q: How do you choose between `map` and `unordered_map`?
interviewBank.answer: Choose `map` when ordered iteration or range queries matter, and `unordered_map` when lookup speed is the priority and order is irrelevant. The hashed version needs a hash function and can degrade under bad hashing.

interviewBank.q: What is iterator invalidation?
interviewBank.answer: An operation that reallocates or restructures the container leaves existing iterators pointing at freed or moved storage. A vector push_back may invalidate all iterators, while a node-based map only invalidates the erased element’s iterator.

interviewBank.answer: Use map when ordered iteration or range queries matter, and unordered_map when average constant lookup matters and order is irrelevant. The hashed version needs a hash function.

interviewBank.q: What invalidates a vector iterator?
interviewBank.answer: Any reallocation, such as a push_back that exceeds capacity, invalidates all iterators and references. Erasing invalidates at and after the erased position.

interviewBank.q: When is std::list a better choice than std::vector?
interviewBank.answer: When elements are inserted or removed in the middle and iterators to other elements must stay valid. Its poor locality usually makes it slower for traversal.

defenseBank.q: Why does `map::operator[]` sometimes create a bug?
defenseBank.answer: It inserts a default-constructed value for a missing key, so a lookup that was meant to be read-only silently grows the container and changes later results.

modules.title: Iterators, Algorithms and Lambdas
modules.goal: Replace hand-written loops with algorithms, pass behaviour as a lambda, and understand iterator invalidation.

topics.title: Algorithms take iterator ranges
topics.body: `std::sort` receives a begin and an end iterator, so it works on any contiguous or random-access range. Half-open ranges mean the end is one past the last element.

topics.title: A lambda is a local function object
topics.body: `[](int x) { return x > 2; }` is an anonymous callable. Captures bring in local state; `[&]` captures by reference and `[=]` by value.

topics.title: accumulate folds a range
topics.body: `std::accumulate` combines the elements with an initial value. The initial value's type is the result type, so `0.0` is needed for a double mean.

topics.title: sort with a lambda comparator
topics.body: The third argument is any callable that answers "does a come before b?". A lambda keeps the rule next to the call, and the sort stays stable only if `stable_sort` is used.

topics.title: accumulate needs the right seed type
topics.body: The initial value fixes the accumulator’s type. Seeding with `0` keeps integer arithmetic even when the range holds doubles, while `0.0` makes the average a real division.

topics.title: find_if takes a predicate
topics.body: It returns the first iterator whose element satisfies the predicate, or `end()` when none does.

topics.title: lower_bound needs sorted input
topics.body: It binary-searches for the first element not less than the value, which is why an unsorted range gives a meaningless answer.

topics.title: remove_if moves the kept values
topics.body: It partitions the range and returns the new logical end; erasing that tail is a separate step.

topics.title: A lambda can capture by reference
topics.body: A reference capture lets the lambda update the caller’s variable, which is how a loop accumulates through an algorithm.

topics.title: reverse reorders in place
topics.body: It swaps from both ends toward the middle, so no extra storage is needed.

interviewBank.q: Why is erase(remove(...)) a two-step operation?
interviewBank.answer: remove_if moves the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end, but it cannot change the container's size because it only sees iterators. erase then removes the tail, which is why both calls are required.

interviewBank.q: What invalidates a vector iterator?
interviewBank.answer: Any reallocation, and any insertion or erase at or before the iterator's position. Reallocation happens on growth, so a stored iterator can dangle after a push_back even if no element was erased.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `find` and `binary_search`?
interviewBank.answer: `find` scans linearly and works on any range, while `binary_search` assumes sorted input and halves the range. Use the latter when the data is already ordered and only presence matters.

interviewBank.q: Why does `remove` not shrink a vector?
interviewBank.answer: It moves the kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end, because it only sees iterators and cannot change the container. The erase-remove idiom removes the tail afterwards.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between capturing by value and by reference?
interviewBank.answer: A by-value capture copies at lambda creation and is const unless the lambda is mutable; a by-reference capture aliases the original and sees later changes. A reference capture must not outlive the variable.

interviewBank.q: Why does erase-remove exist?
interviewBank.answer: std::remove_if only reorders elements and returns the new end, because an algorithm cannot change a container’s size. The container’s erase then removes the tail.

interviewBank.q: What complexity does std::sort guarantee?
interviewBank.answer: O(n log n) comparisons on average and in the worst case for the standard library implementation, with O(log n) extra stack space.

defenseBank.q: When is a hand-written loop clearer than an algorithm?
defenseBank.answer: When the loop performs several different actions in one pass, or the algorithm would need a lambda so complex that the loop is shorter. Algorithms win when they name a single operation.
steps: Name the single operation the loop performs.
Check whether an algorithm states it directly.
Keep the loop when the body does more than one thing.

defenseBank.q: Why do lambdas capture by reference carefully?
defenseBank.answer: A reference capture keeps a pointer to a local that may be gone when the lambda is called later, which is a dangling reference. Capture by value when the lambda outlives the scope.

modules.title: Exception Handling and Error Management
modules.goal: Signal failure with exceptions, catch them at the right level, and keep objects consistent while unwinding.

topics.title: throw, try, catch
topics.body: `throw` transfers control to the nearest matching `catch`. Stack objects are destroyed on the way out, which is what makes RAII the partner of exceptions.

topics.title: A custom exception type
topics.body: Derive from `std::runtime_error` when callers may want to catch a category. The `what()` message should say what failed, not just that something failed.

topics.title: noexcept is a promise
topics.body: `noexcept` states that a function will not throw. If it does, the program terminates, so mark only operations that genuinely cannot fail or must not.

topics.title: Throw by value, catch by const reference
topics.body: The exception object is copied when thrown and caught by reference avoids a second copy, while `const` prevents accidental modification. Catching by value slices derived exceptions.
topics.output: caught: index 9 is past the end

topics.title: RAII cleans up during unwinding
topics.body: When an exception leaves a scope, every fully constructed local object is destroyed. That is why a guard object releases its resource even though the normal exit never runs.

topics.title: Stack unwinding runs destructors
topics.body: When an exception leaves a scope, every constructed local is destroyed before the handler runs, which is how locks and files are released.

topics.title: what() explains a standard exception
topics.body: Every standard exception derives from `std::exception` and carries a message through `what()`.

topics.title: noexcept keeps moves cheap
topics.body: A move constructor marked `noexcept` lets a vector move elements instead of copying them when it grows.

topics.title: try blocks can nest
topics.body: An inner handler can deal with one failure and let the rest propagate to the outer handler.

topics.title: catch(...) takes anything
topics.body: The ellipsis handler catches every type, which is useful as a last resort but hides the actual exception.

interviewBank.q: When should you return an error code instead of throwing?
interviewBank.answer: When failure is expected and cheap to handle at every call site, or when the code is compiled without exceptions. Exceptions fit exceptional failures that cannot be handled locally.

interviewBank.q: What does exception safety mean?
interviewBank.answer: That an operation leaves the program in a valid state when it throws: no leaks, no half-updated invariants. The strong guarantee adds that the operation either fully succeeds or changes nothing.

interviewBank.q: What does `noexcept` promise?
interviewBank.answer: That the function will not let an exception escape; if one does, `std::terminate` runs. It lets containers and the optimizer assume safety, which is why move constructors are usually marked noexcept.

interviewBank.q: When should an exception not be used?
interviewBank.answer: For expected, frequent conditions such as "not found" where a return value or `std::optional` is clearer and cheaper. Exceptions are for exceptional failure that the immediate caller cannot handle.

interviewBank.q: What are the three exception-safety guarantees?
interviewBank.answer: The basic guarantee leaves the program valid but unspecified, the strong guarantee is all-or-nothing, and the no-throw guarantee promises no exception escapes.

interviewBank.q: When should an error not be an exception?
interviewBank.answer: When it is expected and handled locally, such as "not found", where a return value or optional is clearer and cheaper than unwinding.

interviewBank.q: Why catch by const reference?
interviewBank.answer: It avoids copying the exception object and prevents slicing a derived exception into a base value, while const stops accidental modification.

defenseBank.q: Why catch by const reference?
defenseBank.answer: A reference preserves the dynamic type for the handler and avoids a copy; const states that the handler does not modify the exception. Catching by value slices a derived exception.
steps: Show the derived-to-base conversion.

Write the catch clause with const&.

defenseBank.q: Why not use exceptions for ordinary control flow?
defenseBank.answer: Throwing is expensive compared to a return, and it hides control flow from a reader. A loop that exits by exception is harder to reason about than one with a condition.

interviewBank.q: Why check is_open instead of assuming the file exists?
interviewBank.answer: Opening can fail for permissions, a missing directory or a locked file, and a failed stream stays in a failed state. Reading it yields nothing, so the program continues with empty data unless the open is checked.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a text and a binary stream?
interviewBank.answer: A text stream may translate line endings, while a binary stream reads and writes the bytes exactly. Use binary for serialized structures, images or anything whose bytes must round-trip unchanged.

interviewBank.q: Why check a stream after opening it?
interviewBank.answer: A failed open leaves the stream in a failed state and every extraction returns immediately, so the program silently works with empty data. `is_open()` or a boolean test turns that into an explicit error path.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between text and binary mode?
interviewBank.answer: Text mode may translate line endings on some platforms, while binary mode reads the exact bytes. Structured records should be read and written in binary with fixed layouts.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between text and binary file mode?
interviewBank.answer: Text mode may translate line endings on some platforms, while binary mode reads and writes the exact bytes. Structured records should use binary mode.

interviewBank.q: Why does an ofstream need to be destroyed or flushed before reading?
interviewBank.answer: Buffered writes may still be in memory; the destructor or flush pushes them to the file. Reading before that can see an incomplete file.

interviewBank.q: Why should a file stream be checked after opening?
interviewBank.answer: A failed open leaves the stream in a failed state and extractions return immediately, so the program silently works with empty data unless is_open is checked.

modules.title: Modern C++ and Version Evolution
modules.goal: Use the features that changed everyday C++: auto, nullptr, range-for, optional, structured bindings and constexpr.

topics.title: auto and nullptr
topics.body: `auto` deduces from the initializer; `nullptr` is a typed null pointer constant, unlike `NULL` which is an integer. Overload resolution can tell them apart.

topics.title: Range-for and structured bindings
topics.body: `for (const auto& [key, value] : map)` names both halves of a pair without `first` and `second`, which makes loops over maps readable.

topics.title: optional models absence
topics.body: `std::optional<T>` either holds a value or holds nothing, which is clearer than a sentinel. Check it before use; `value()` throws when empty.

topics.title: optional expresses a value that may be missing
topics.body: `std::optional<T>` either holds a T or holds nothing, so "not found" needs no magic number. `value_or` supplies a default without a branch.

topics.title: Structured bindings walk a map
topics.body: Binding `[name, age]` to each map entry avoids the `first`/`second` noise, and the reference keeps the iteration from copying the pair.

topics.title: Structured bindings unpack a pair
topics.body: One declaration names both halves of a pair or tuple, which removes the `first`/`second` noise from loops.

topics.title: auto drops top-level const
topics.body: Deduction copies the value and discards the top-level qualifier, so `auto` from a const int gives an int; `const auto&` keeps it.

topics.title: nullptr replaces NULL
topics.body: It has its own type and converts to any pointer without being mistaken for the integer zero by an overload.

topics.title: if constexpr selects at compile time
topics.body: The false branch is discarded during instantiation, so it can contain code that would not compile for that type.

topics.title: optional avoids a sentinel
topics.body: The type states that a value may be absent, so no legal value has to be reserved as "not found".

interviewBank.q: Why is nullptr better than NULL?
interviewBank.answer: `nullptr` has its own type, so it converts to any pointer type without becoming an integer. `NULL` is usually 0, which can select an int overload and hide a bug.

interviewBank.q: When should a function return optional instead of a pointer?
interviewBank.answer: When absence is a normal outcome and the value is small or cheap to move. A pointer suggests an object already exists somewhere; optional suggests the function may produce one or none.

interviewBank.q: When is `std::optional` better than a sentinel like -1?
interviewBank.answer: When every value of the type is legal, so no sentinel can be reserved. The type then states the possibility of absence and the compiler forces the caller to handle it.

interviewBank.q: What does `if constexpr` solve?
interviewBank.answer: It discards the untaken branch during instantiation, so a template can use operations that are valid for some types but not others. A plain `if` still has to compile both branches.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between auto and decltype?
interviewBank.answer: auto deduces a value type after dropping references and top-level const; decltype preserves the exact declared type, including references.

interviewBank.q: When does structured binding copy instead of reference?
interviewBank.answer: Writing auto [a, b] copies; auto& [a, b] binds references. Copying is fine for small values but silently detaches from the source.

interviewBank.q: Why is std::optional not a replacement for error codes?
interviewBank.answer: It expresses absence, not the reason for failure. When the caller needs to distinguish causes, a variant or an exception carries more information.

defenseBank.q: How do you decide which C++ standard a project targets?
defenseBank.answer: By the compiler support the deployment actually has and the features the code needs, not by the newest standard. Pin the flag, test it in CI and document the requirement.
steps: Check the compiler's supported standards.
List the features the code relies on.
Pin the standard flag and state it in the README.

defenseBank.q: Why label C++23 and C++26 features explicitly?
defenseBank.answer: Support varies by compiler version, so a feature that compiles locally can fail elsewhere. The label tells the reader which flag and which compiler were verified.

learn.title: auto and nullptr
learn.body: `auto` deduces from the initializer; `nullptr` is a typed null pointer constant, unlike `NULL` which is an integer. Overload resolution can tell them apart.

learn.title: Range-for and structured bindings
learn.body: `for (const auto& [key, value] : map)` names both halves of a pair without `first` and `second`, which makes loops over maps readable.

learn.title: optional models absence
learn.body: `std::optional<T>` either holds a value or holds nothing, which is clearer than a sentinel. Check it before use; `value()` throws when empty.

learn.title: optional expresses a value that may be missing
learn.body: `std::optional<T>` either holds a T or holds nothing, so "not found" needs no magic number. `value_or` supplies a default without a branch.

learn.title: Structured bindings walk a map
learn.body: Binding `[name, age]` to each map entry avoids the `first`/`second` noise, and the reference keeps the iteration from copying the pair.

learn.title: Structured bindings unpack a pair
learn.body: One declaration names both halves of a pair or tuple, which removes the `first`/`second` noise from loops.

learn.title: auto drops top-level const
learn.body: Deduction copies the value and discards the top-level qualifier, so `auto` from a const int gives an int; `const auto&` keeps it.

learn.title: nullptr replaces NULL
learn.body: It has its own type and converts to any pointer without being mistaken for the integer zero by an overload.

learn.title: if constexpr selects at compile time
learn.body: The false branch is discarded during instantiation, so it can contain code that would not compile for that type.

learn.title: optional avoids a sentinel
learn.body: The type states that a value may be absent, so no legal value has to be reserved as "not found".

Why is nullptr better than NULL?
interview.answer: `nullptr` has its own type, so it converts to any pointer type without becoming an integer. `NULL` is usually 0, which can select an int overload and hide a bug.

interview.q: When should a function return optional instead of a pointer?
interview.answer: When absence is a normal outcome and the value is small or cheap to move. A pointer suggests an object already exists somewhere; optional suggests the function may produce one or none.

interview.q: When is `std::optional` better than a sentinel like -1?
interview.answer: When every value of the type is legal, so no sentinel can be reserved. The type then states the possibility of absence and the compiler forces the caller to handle it.

interview.q: What does `if constexpr` solve?
interview.answer: It discards the untaken branch during instantiation, so a template can use operations that are valid for some types but not others. A plain `if` still has to compile both branches.

interview.q: What is the difference between auto and decltype?
interview.answer: auto deduces a value type after dropping references and top-level const; decltype preserves the exact declared type, including references.

interview.q: When does structured binding copy instead of reference?
interview.answer: Writing auto [a, b] copies; auto& [a, b] binds references. Copying is fine for small values but silently detaches from the source.

interview.q: Why is std::optional not a replacement for error codes?
interview.answer: It expresses absence, not the reason for failure. When the caller needs to distinguish causes, a variant or an exception carries more information.

modules.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
modules.goal: Analyse complexity, implement core algorithms, and choose a data structure from the operations the problem needs.

topics.title: Big O describes growth
topics.body: Big O counts how work grows with input, ignoring constants: a linear scan is O(n), a halving search is O(log n). Two algorithms can both be correct and differ by orders of magnitude at size.

topics.title: Binary search halves the range
topics.body: On a sorted array, compare with the middle and discard the half that cannot contain the target. The loop runs O(log n) times; the overflow-safe midpoint is `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.

topics.title: Dynamic programming remembers
topics.body: Tabulation stores each subproblem once, turning an exponential recursion into a linear pass. The array is the memory of answers already computed.

topics.title: Iterative Fibonacci is linear
topics.body: Keeping the last two values in a loop needs constant extra space and no call stack. The recursive version recomputes the same subproblems unless it is memoised.

topics.title: Linear search scans every element
topics.body: It stops at the first match and is the only option when the data is unsorted; worst case is one pass.

topics.title: Selection sort picks the minimum each pass
topics.body: It scans the unsorted tail for the smallest value and swaps it into place, which is O(n²) but uses no extra memory.

topics.title: Merging two sorted ranges is linear
topics.body: Two pointers advance through the inputs, always taking the smaller head, which is the combine step of merge sort.

topics.title: A stack is last in, first out
topics.body: The most recent push is the first pop, which is why stacks model undo, recursion and expression evaluation.

topics.title: A queue is first in, first out
topics.body: The earliest push leaves first, which is the shape of scheduling and breadth-first traversal.

topics.title: A hash map trades order for speed
topics.body: Average lookup is constant and keys are unordered, which is the right trade when only membership matters.

interviewBank.q: How do you choose between a hash map and a balanced tree?
interviewBank.answer: A hash map gives average constant lookup but no ordering. A balanced tree gives O(log n) lookup with sorted iteration and range queries. Choose by whether order is part of the problem.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between O(n log n) and O(n)?
interviewBank.answer: A linear pass touches each element once; a sort-based solution does logarithmic work per element. At a million elements the difference is a factor of about twenty.

interviewBank.q: What is the time complexity of binary search and why?
interviewBank.answer: O(log n), because every comparison halves the candidate range. A range of a million elements needs about twenty comparisons.

interviewBank.q: When is a hash map preferable to sorting plus binary search?
interviewBank.answer: When the data changes often and many lookups are expected, since a hash map gives average O(1) lookup without re-sorting. Sorting wins when ordered traversal or range queries are also needed.

interviewBank.q: What does Big O describe?
interviewBank.answer: An upper bound on how running time or memory grows with input size, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It compares algorithms, not machines.

interviewBank.q: When is dynamic programming applicable?
interviewBank.answer: When a problem has overlapping subproblems and an optimal substructure, so caching a subproblem’s result avoids recomputation.

interviewBank.q: Why can BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
interviewBank.answer: It explores vertices in order of distance from the source, so the first time a vertex is reached is by a shortest path.

defenseBank.q: How do you explain an algorithm's complexity in an interview?
defenseBank.answer: Name the operation that dominates, count how many times it runs as a function of n, and state the space the algorithm needs beyond its input.
steps: Identify the nested or repeated operation.
Express its count in terms of n.
State the auxiliary space.

defenseBank.q: Why start with brute force before optimizing?
defenseBank.answer: It proves you understand the problem and gives a correct baseline to test the faster version against. The optimization then has a reference answer and a measured reason.

modules.title: Multithreading and Concurrency
modules.goal: Start and join a thread, protect shared data with a mutex, and know why a data race is undefined behaviour.

topics.title: A thread must be joined or detached
topics.body: `std::thread` starts running immediately. Its destructor terminates the program unless the thread was joined or detached first.

topics.title: A mutex serialises access
topics.body: Two threads incrementing the same counter race unless the read-modify-write is protected. `std::lock_guard` locks on construction and unlocks on destruction, including on exceptions.

topics.title: atomic for a single value
topics.body: `std::atomic<int>` makes one read-modify-write indivisible without a mutex. It does not make a whole data structure thread-safe.

topics.title: atomic removes the lost update
topics.body: A plain int incremented from two threads is a data race: read, add and write can interleave. `std::atomic<int>` makes the increment one indivisible operation, so the total is exact.

topics.title: detach lets a thread run independently
topics.body: A detached thread owns itself and cannot be joined; the program must not exit while it still reads shared state.

topics.title: lock_guard releases at scope exit
topics.body: The mutex is unlocked by the guard’s destructor, so an early return or exception cannot leave it locked.

topics.title: A condition_variable waits for a signal
topics.body: The waiter releases the lock while asleep and reacquires it before returning, which avoids burning a core.

topics.title: atomic load reads one snapshot
topics.body: A relaxed load returns the current value without a lock, which is enough for a single counter.

topics.title: async returns a future
topics.body: The task runs on another thread and `get()` blocks until its result is ready, propagating any exception.

topics.title: A data race is undefined behaviour
topics.body: Two unsynchronised accesses with one write are not merely unpredictable; the standard says nothing about the result, so the fix is synchronisation, not testing.

interviewBank.q: What is a data race?
interviewBank.answer: Two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, and there is no synchronisation ordering them. In C++ that is undefined behaviour, not just an unexpected value.

interviewBank.q: Why is a mutex not a complete concurrency design?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps one critical section correct but introduces contention and deadlock risk, and it does not make a compound operation across several calls atomic. The design has to define the invariant and which lock owns it.

interviewBank.q: What does a mutex actually protect?
interviewBank.answer: It protects the invariant that the locked region is supposed to maintain, not the variable by itself. Every access to the shared state must take the same lock or the protocol is broken.

interviewBank.answer:
Output:

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a race condition and a data race?
interviewBank.answer: A data race is two unsynchronised accesses with a write, which is undefined behaviour. A race condition is a timing-dependent logic bug, which can exist even with atomics.

interviewBank.q: How do you prevent deadlock between two mutexes?
interviewBank.answer: Acquire them in a single consistent order, or use std::scoped_lock, which locks multiple mutexes without deadlock.

interviewBank.q: When is std::atomic enough instead of a mutex?
interviewBank.answer: When a single value is updated independently, such as a counter or flag. If an invariant spans several variables, a mutex is needed to protect the whole update.

interviewBank.q: What does scoped_lock protect here?
interviewBank.answer:
Output:
both
scoped_lock locks both mutexes without deadlock and releases them at the end of the block.

defenseBank.q: How do you prevent deadlock between two mutexes?
defenseBank.answer: Always acquire them in the same global order, or lock both at once with std::scoped_lock, which uses a deadlock-avoiding algorithm.
steps: List the locks a thread takes.
Impose one order on every path.
Prefer scoped_lock when both are needed together.

defenseBank.q: Why does a race sometimes pass tests?
defenseBank.answer: Its outcome depends on timing, so a run on one machine can happen to serialise the accesses. Passing once says nothing; the absence of synchronisation is the bug.

modules.title: Professional Engineering and Testing
modules.goal: Structure a project, assert what the code promises, and use the compiler's warnings and sanitizers as tools.

topics.title: The standard you compiled with
topics.body: `__cplusplus` reports the language standard the compiler used. If it prints 201703, the build is C++17; a modern feature compiled without the right flag fails here first.

topics.title: assert states a precondition
topics.body: `assert` checks a condition in debug builds and is removed with NDEBUG. It documents what must be true and fails loudly instead of corrupting data.

topics.title: static_assert checks at compile time
topics.body: `static_assert` runs during compilation, so a violated assumption stops the build with your message. It is the cheapest test to run and the hardest to skip.

topics.title: Rule of Zero
topics.body: A class that owns its members through RAII types needs no destructor, copy constructor or assignment operator; the compiler-generated ones are correct. That is less code and fewer chances to get lifetime wrong.

topics.title: A move-only class
topics.body: Deleting the copy operations makes ownership exclusive explicit: the unique_ptr member cannot be copied, and `std::move` transfers it. This is the type-system version of "there is only one owner".

topics.title: A header guard prevents double inclusion
topics.body: The `#ifndef`/`#define` pair makes the second inclusion a no-op, which is why a header can be included from several files.

topics.title: Assertions document an invariant
topics.body: The check runs in debug builds and disappears with `NDEBUG`, so it documents an invariant without costing release performance.

topics.title: Sanitizers catch memory bugs
topics.body: Compiling with `-fsanitize=address` reports an out-of-bounds access at the point it happens; the flag is a build decision, not a code change.

topics.title: A unit test pins behaviour
topics.body: A test states the expected result and fails loudly when the implementation drifts, which is cheaper than a manual check.

topics.title: A commit records one change
topics.body: A small, reviewable commit with a message that states the intent is what makes history useful later.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between assert and an exception?
interviewBank.answer: An assertion documents an internal precondition that should never be false and is removed in release builds. An exception reports a runtime failure that callers are expected to handle, such as invalid input.

interviewBank.q: Why compile with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic?
interviewBank.answer: They surface uninitialised reads, unused results, narrowing conversions and non-standard extensions before they become runtime bugs. A warning-clean build is cheaper than finding the same defect in production.

interviewBank.q: What does the Rule of Five add to the Rule of Three?
interviewBank.answer: Move construction and move assignment, so a resource can be transferred instead of copied. A class that declares one of the five should consider all five.

interviewBank.q: Why is `const` correctness a design tool rather than decoration?
interviewBank.answer: It encodes which operations may mutate state, so the compiler rejects accidental writes and the interface documents itself. It also enables passing by const reference without losing the ability to call readers.

interviewBank.answer:

interviewBank.answer:

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a header guard and #pragma once?
interviewBank.answer: A guard is standard and portable but must use a unique macro; #pragma once is shorter and supported by every major compiler but not part of the standard.

interviewBank.q: What does a sanitizer catch that a normal build does not?
interviewBank.answer: AddressSanitizer detects out-of-bounds and use-after-free; UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer reports signed overflow and invalid shifts. Both instrument the build and slow it down.

interviewBank.q: Why is a failing unit test more useful than a manual check?
interviewBank.answer: It states the expected behaviour in code, runs on every change, and pinpoints the regression instead of relying on someone remembering to click through the app.

defenseBank.q: How do you structure a small C++ project?
defenseBank.answer: Headers declare the interfaces, one source file per implementation, and a build file lists the targets. Keep main thin so the logic can be tested without it.
steps: Separate declarations from definitions.
Keep one responsibility per translation unit.
Put the executable's entry point in its own file.

defenseBank.q: What does the One Definition Rule forbid?
defenseBank.answer: Two different definitions of the same function or object in one program. Declarations can repeat, definitions cannot, which is why headers hold declarations and source files hold bodies.

modules.title: Projects, Design Patterns and Career
modules.goal: Assemble the course into a portfolio project, apply a pattern where it earns its place, and explain your code in an interview.

topics.title: A project is a set of responsibilities
topics.body: Split a console application into input, domain rules and storage. Each part can then be tested and replaced without rewriting the others.

topics.title: Singleton only when one instance is the rule
topics.body: A private constructor plus a static accessor enforces one instance. Use it for a genuinely singular resource; otherwise it becomes hidden global state that tests cannot replace.

topics.title: Two pointers in an interview
topics.body: A sorted pair-sum uses one index at each end: move the left up when the sum is too small, the right down when it is too large. Linear time, constant extra space.

topics.title: A factory hides the concrete type
topics.body: The caller asks for a shape and receives a base pointer, so adding a new shape does not touch the call site.

topics.title: An observer is notified by its subject
topics.body: The subject keeps a list of listeners and calls each one when its state changes, which decouples the two sides.

topics.title: A strategy is a swappable algorithm
topics.body: The behaviour is injected as a callable, so the caller can change the algorithm without editing the class.

topics.title: A builder assembles step by step
topics.body: The builder collects the parts and produces the finished object once, which keeps the constructor from taking ten arguments.

topics.title: An adapter fits an old interface
topics.body: It translates one interface into the one the caller expects, so old code can be reused without rewriting it.

topics.title: A singleton owns its only instance
topics.body: The instance is a function-local static, which is created on first use and destroyed at exit.

topics.title: SOLID keeps a class focused
topics.body: A class with one reason to change is easier to test; the report below formats, while the caller decides where it goes.

interviewBank.q: How do you present a project in a 5-minute interview?
interviewBank.answer: Problem, constraints, the one design decision that mattered, the result with a number, and one thing you would change. The rest belongs in the repository README.

interviewBank.q: When is a design pattern unnecessary complexity?
interviewBank.answer: When there is only one implementation and no sign of a second: a factory for one type or an observer with one listener adds indirection without a decision to make. Patterns pay for variation.

Output:
5

interviewBank.q: What does the single-responsibility principle ask for?
interviewBank.answer: One reason to change per class, so a class has one job. That keeps tests focused and limits the blast radius of a change.

interviewBank.q: When does a design pattern become unnecessary complexity?
interviewBank.answer: When the variation it prepares for does not exist. A factory or strategy with one implementation adds indirection without buying flexibility.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer composition over inheritance for reuse?
interviewBank.answer: It couples to behaviour rather than a type hierarchy, so the part can be swapped and tested independently. Inheritance is for a genuine is-a contract.

interviewBank.q: What does the builder produce?

Output:
marks:3
Each builder step returns the same object, so the chain finishes with one configured report.

The subject holds three listeners, so all three receive the notification.

defenseBank.q: Why is Singleton criticised despite being common?
defenseBank.answer: It is global state with a constructor, so tests cannot substitute it and dependencies are hidden. A passed-in object with an interface gives the same single instance without the coupling.
steps: Name the hidden dependency.

defenseBank.q: What makes a C++ portfolio project credible?
defenseBank.answer: It builds with one documented command, has tests for the core rules, handles bad input and explains its trade-offs. A small finished project beats a large half-written one.

learn.title: A project is a set of responsibilities
learn.body: Split a console application into input, domain rules and storage. Each part can then be tested and replaced without rewriting the others.

learn.title: Singleton only when one instance is the rule
learn.body: A private constructor plus a static accessor enforces one instance. Use it for a genuinely singular resource; otherwise it becomes hidden global state that tests cannot replace.

learn.title: Two pointers in an interview
learn.body: A sorted pair-sum uses one index at each end: move the left up when the sum is too small, the right down when it is too large. Linear time, constant extra space.

learn.title: A factory hides the concrete type
learn.body: The caller asks for a shape and receives a base pointer, so adding a new shape does not touch the call site.

learn.title: An observer is notified by its subject
learn.body: The subject keeps a list of listeners and calls each one when its state changes, which decouples the two sides.

learn.title: A strategy is a swappable algorithm
learn.body: The behaviour is injected as a callable, so the caller can change the algorithm without editing the class.

learn.title: A builder assembles step by step
learn.body: The builder collects the parts and produces the finished object once, which keeps the constructor from taking ten arguments.

learn.title: An adapter fits an old interface
learn.body: It translates one interface into the one the caller expects, so old code can be reused without rewriting it.

learn.title: A singleton owns its only instance
learn.body: The instance is a function-local static, which is created on first use and destroyed at exit.

learn.title: SOLID keeps a class focused
learn.body: A class with one reason to change is easier to test; the report below formats, while the caller decides where it goes.
